events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.
Priya proposes Priya, Leo. I include myself because I know my mission card will be Success, and Leo is a reasonable partner for the first mission to test cooperation.

I support the proposal of Priya and me for mission one. Let me lay out my reasoning plainly, since I have no special information to offer.

First, the math: with five players, mission one needs a team of two. Priya has proposed herself plus me, which is a legal size, and it is the only combination I would be equally comfortable with. On the first mission there is no information about who plays evil, so the only real goals are to get a team through and to learn something from the result.

Second, on Priya's statement. She says she knows her mission card is Success. I have no way to verify that, and honestly I do not need to. Mission cards are secret by design, and if I demanded to see or trust her claim before voting, I would be playing the wrong game entirely. What I do know is that she volunteered a card claim openly before any vote, which is the behavior of someone trying to build a credible coalition rather than someone trying to obscure their alignment. I am recording her claim as an untested claim, not as established fact.

Third, my own position. I am a loyal servant with no knowledge of anyone's role, including my own hidden from me. I am one of the two most predictable players at this table, and that is exactly why I think being on a two-person mission one team is acceptable. If Priya's claim is right, we succeed and the game moves on. If it is wrong, we fail together and we learn that we cannot trust Priya's early claims, which is genuinely valuable information for the rest of the game. Either way the downside is small and the information gain is real.

Fourth, the alternative. Rejecting this team costs us the leader's proposal and gives leadership to someone else for no clear gain. The cost of a rejection is high and the cost of a possible first-mission fail is only one of three. I would only consider pushing back if I had evidence, and I have none.

Priya, a direct question on the specific point you raised: you mentioned Leo as a "reasonable partner" for testing cooperation. What exactly did you have in mind that you think I bring to a two-person mission, and did anything about the order of this proposal or the timing of your claim come from information you have that I do not?

Leo, direct answer: I have no private information about you, and nothing about the order or timing of my proposal came from hidden knowledge. I am a Loyal Servant, so I know only that I must play Success. I proposed myself because mission one needs two players and I can vouch for my own card; I chose you because your public behavior so far is measured, transparent, and open to being tested. By “reasonable partner” I meant exactly that: someone whose conduct gives the table something to judge, not someone I claim to have cleared. If this team is approved, the mission result tells us whether that trust was justified. If it fails, then my proposal was wrong and the table should hold me to that. I am not offering an accusation against anyone, and I do not need a reply from you here.

Priya's answer closed out the point I raised, so I will not re-ask it. To be clear about what I do and do not treat as established: Priya claims a Success card, and she claims to be a Loyal Servant. I have no way to confirm either claim, and I am recording both as untested. What her answer did give me is that her selection criteria were visible behavior rather than hidden knowledge, which is a checkable criterion and therefore a better foundation than a secret alliance.

On my own reasoning for mission one. With five players and two seats needed, Priya plus me is a legal and, on current information, sensible team. Nobody at this table has yet demonstrated anything about anyone else, so the honest position is that I am pairing with the only player who has volunteered a claim and explained it consistently. That is a weak signal, but it is a signal, and refusing to cooperate on the basis of no signal at all would cost us a mission for no informational gain.

I also want to name the risk I am accepting, so it is on the record. If Priya is actually Evil, then two of the two seats on mission one are one Good and one Evil, and we fail. That would be a direct hit against my proposal support. The mitigation is that mission one failing is not decisive; we have three failures needed for Evil to win, and a failed first mission plus a revealed bad claim is worth far more than a silent first mission that teaches us nothing.

The alternative to approving is not a safer team. It is a new leader, a new proposal, and the same absence of information. Rejecting here trades a small known risk for a known delay.

So I support Priya and Leo for mission one, without reservation and without pretending the claim is proven. I have no accusation against Arjun, Theo, or Noah, and I have no information that would justify one. If this team is approved and the mission fails, I will want the table to examine why, and my own vote for it should be weighed accordingly.

I support Priya and Leo for mission one. Leo's point holds: with five players and two seats, this is a legal team, and nothing public yet justifies blocking it. Priya's card claim is still only a claim, so the table should judge her by the mission result rather than by her word. I am not accusing anyone here. If the mission succeeds, we gain a useful data point. If it fails, we should examine the team carefully, and I want that result as much as anyone. I am judging this team on the public record, and on that record it is acceptable.

I also support Priya and Leo for mission one. On the public record, this team is a legal two-player proposal from the sitting leader, and nothing has been said that justifies a rejection. Priya volunteered a clear card claim, Leo has walked through his reasoning openly, and Theo has already noted the right standard: judge the team by the mission result, not by anyone's word. On mission one with no prior data, the cost of rejecting is a new leader and a new proposal with the same absence of information, while the cost of approving is at most one of three possible failures. That trade favors approval. I have no accusation to make against anyone at this table at this point, and I do not want my silence to be read as one. I am approving Priya and Leo for mission one and I will judge the result honestly when we see it.

I am still supporting Priya and Leo for mission one. Nothing new has come up since my earlier statement that would change the picture. Priya's card claim is untested, and so is Leo's reasoning, so the mission result is the only real evidence we will get. I am not blaming anyone here, and I will vote approve on the current team so we can gather that information and move on.

Third and final speaking turn of mine on this proposal, and my position has not moved: I vote to approve Priya and Leo for mission one.

Let me consolidate rather than repeat. The table has now spoken. Priya made a specific, checkable claim, defended it when asked, and explained her selection criterion in terms of observable conduct rather than hidden knowledge. I pressed her on that point and she answered directly, which is exactly what I was looking for. Leo — that was me, I am the Leo on this team — reasoned openly and named the risk he was accepting before the mission ran, not after. Theo and Arjun have both said the same thing from different angles: nothing in the public record justifies blocking a legal two-player team from the sitting leader, and the mission result is the evidence that matters, not anyone's word. I agree with both of them.

The arithmetic is unchanged and I want it on the record one more time. Mission one needs two players out of five. Priya and me is legal. The cost of rejecting is a new leader, a new proposal, and the same total absence of information, plus one of the five rejections Evil needs. The cost of approving is at most one of the three failures Evil needs, and we would gain a genuine data point either way. Approve is the better trade.

What I am explicitly not doing: I am not accusing Priya. Her card claim remains untested, and a claim that has been stated openly, consistently, and with a stated basis is more credible than a card claim that was never made. If she turns out to be wrong, the mission result will tell us, and the table should hold her to it then. That is a standard for everyone, not a special one for her.

I also have nothing to say against Arjun, Theo, or Noah. Nobody has said anything that would justify an accusation, and I will not manufacture one to look decisive. Silence from me on those three should not be read as suspicion.

So: Priya and Leo, mission one. Approve. Let us get the result and learn something from it.

I have stayed quiet so far, so let me put my position on the record. I am inclined to approve Priya and Leo for mission one.

The reasoning I find compelling is the same one the table has already converged on. This is a legal two-player proposal from the sitting leader, the first mission of the game, and nobody has produced a single piece of evidence against anyone. Priya volunteered a card claim before any vote was cast and defended it directly when Leo pressed her, which is more accountability than the minimum. Leo laid out his reasoning, named the specific risk he was accepting, and has not tried to hide it. That is the kind of open conduct I want to see more of, and punishing it with a rejection on mission one would teach the wrong lesson.

I have thought about whether a first-mission fail is worth the information. It is not, in my view. One fail out of three is a real cost, and the information it would buy is thin: a two-person mission that fails implicates both members, but we would learn nothing about the other three of us, which is where the real question lies. Rejecting the team does not avoid that cost anyway; it just hands leadership to someone else facing the identical absence of information, plus it burns one of five rejections. Approve is the better trade.

To be explicit about the other three: I have nothing against Priya beyond her untested claim, which is a neutral fact at this stage, and I have no accusation against Arjun, Theo, or anyone else. I will not manufacture suspicion just to sound engaged. If this mission fails, the table should look hard at both team members, and I will want that examination as much as anyone. If it succeeds, we take the data point and move to the three-player mission, where the choices get harder and I expect we will need the goodwill and clear standards being set here today.

So my vote is approve on Priya and Leo. Let us get a result and give this table something real to work with.

This is my final statement on the proposal. I still approve Priya and Leo for mission one. The team is legal, and nobody has offered evidence against either member. Priya's card claim is untested, and so is Leo's reasoning, so the mission result is the best evidence we will get. I am not accusing anyone, and I will vote approve so the table can gather that result and move forward.

Priya confirms Priya, Leo. The discussion produced no new evidence against either member, and Priya and Leo remain the legal team with the clearest public reasoning for mission one. I will keep the lineup.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 1 succeeds (0 fail cards).

Arjun proposes Arjun, Priya, Leo. As leader for mission two I need a three-player team. The only players I have reason to trust from the public record are Priya and Leo, who both demonstrated open reasoning on mission one, and I include myself as a third confirmed-good seat. This lineup excludes the two players I have most reason to doubt and gives the table a team built on demonstrated conduct rather than untested claims. Mission one succeeded cleanly, so keeping the cooperative core together is the safest path to a second data point.

I support Arjun, Priya, Leo for mission two, but I want the record accurate. Mission one succeeded with Priya and Leo, and I know I submitted Success; that is a real data point for me, not proof of Leo’s allegiance. Arjun is the sitting leader, the proposal is legal, and I have no evidence against Theo or Noah that would justify blocking it. However, Arjun’s phrase “third confirmed-good seat” overstates the public record: mission one did not test Arjun at all, and no public result confirms any individual beyond the fact that the team produced zero fail cards. I am not accusing Arjun; I am asking him to clarify the basis for that phrase, because if it means he is treating himself as confirmed without evidence, the table should know. Arjun, what exactly did you mean by “confirmed-good seat”—are you claiming private knowledge of your own loyalty, or are you asking us to infer confirmation from the public record, and if the latter, what specifically confirms you?

Priya, direct answer to your question: "confirmed-good seat" was loose language on my part and you are right to press it. I am not claiming private knowledge of my own loyalty, and I have none to claim. What I meant was that I am proposing myself as a seat I can vouch for in the ordinary sense: I know what I submitted on mission one when I was not on the team — nothing, because I was not on it — and I know my own intentions going into mission two. That is self-knowledge, not public confirmation, and I should not have used a word that implies the table has verified me. It has not. Nobody has verified me, and I will not pretend otherwise.

The correction does not change the proposal. Arjun, Priya, Leo is a legal three-player team for mission two, built on the only conduct this table has actually observed: Priya made a clear claim, defended it under direct questioning from Leo, and the mission returned zero fail cards; Leo reasoned openly, named his own risk in advance, and asked a real question rather than performing one. I include myself because I am the leader and I will be playing a Success card. That is three seats where the public record gives us something, and it is still a record, not a verdict.

I want to be careful about what I am not saying. I am not claiming Theo or Noah are guilty. I have no evidence against either of them, and if I accused them I would be doing exactly what I just admitted I should not do: dressing up inference as confirmation. Mission one tested two of us and cleared them on the result. Missions two and three are where the table actually learns anything about the three who sat out, and I would rather arrive at those missions with a clean, cooperative core than with a lineup assembled to spread suspicion around.

So: my phrase was overstated, Priya's push was fair, and I withdraw the wording. The team stands as proposed. If the table wants to test Theo and Noah, mission three and mission four give us room to do that deliberately rather than by exclusion here. I vote approve on Arjun, Priya, Leo and I will judge the result honestly when it comes.

I vote to approve Arjun, Priya, Leo for mission two, and I want to say why in terms of the record rather than my feelings. First, I appreciate Arjun's correction. "Confirmed-good seat" was wrong wording, and he withdrew it directly rather than defending it, which is worth noting. The corrected version — that he is including himself as a seat he can vouch for from his own intentions, with no public verification — is honest, and it is the same standard I applied to myself when I backed Priya on mission one. I have no private knowledge of my own alignment beyond knowing I must play Success, so I do not get to hold others to a stronger basis for self-vouching than I can meet myself. Second, the mission arithmetic. Five players, mission two needs three seats. Arjun, Priya, Leo is legal, it keeps the only two players the table has actually tested together, and it costs us nothing in rejections. The alternative is not a safer team; it is a different three names with the same absence of information about Theo and Noah, plus one of the five rejections we can afford only four of. Third, what the mission result will and will not tell us. If this team succeeds, we will know a three-player team including me passed cleanly, which says nothing about anyone not on it. If it fails, that implicates all three of us, and I will want the table to examine each of us honestly rather than assume the two who proposed are the two at fault. I am also aware that Priya's claim from mission one is now backed by a result, and mine is not: I was on that team and the result does not verify me personally. I hold that both facts are true. Fourth, on the two players sitting out. I am not claiming Theo or Noah are Evil. Nobody has produced a single piece of evidence against either of them, and I will not manufacture an accusation to sound decisive. But excluding someone twice in a row has its own cost: it means we learn nothing about them until the team gets large enough to include them, and on mission three we will be choosing between a three-seat team and a two-seat team, so the pressure to guess at untested players grows. I would rather that pressure be applied deliberately and with reasons on the record. To that end, Theo, I am asking you directly and specifically: you have been on the table for two discussions and have not been on either mission team, and you voted reject on mission one despite publicly saying you supported Priya and Leo. I want to understand that. What is your actual read on the current lineup, and if you think Arjun, Priya, Leo is wrong for mission two, what is the specific reason and what team would you put up instead? I am asking because your answer is more useful to me than

Leo, you asked me directly about my vote, so here is my answer. In discussion I said I approved Priya and Leo, but on the ballot I voted reject. That mismatch is my responsibility. I should have said plainly that I was uneasy about a two-player team resting on an untested card claim, and I did not. For mission two, I will vote approve on Arjun, Priya, Leo. The team is legal, Arjun has withdrawn the phrase 'confirmed-good seat,' and mission one produced a clean result that gives no grounds to block a lineup now. I am not accusing anyone. I am judging this team on the public record, and I will judge the mission result honestly when it comes.

Theo, thank you for answering my question directly. A public statement that does not match a ballot is a real failure of accountability, and you owned it plainly instead of papering over it. That is worth more to me than a perfect speech would have been, and I am recording that your position on Arjun, Priya, Leo for mission two is now approve.

With that settled, my position is unchanged: I approve Arjun, Priya, Leo for mission two.

First, what changed since my last turn. Arjun withdrew the phrase "confirmed-good seat" and gave me the corrected version: self-knowledge of his own intentions, not public verification. He also said he would not accuse Theo or Noah of being Evil, and that if the table wants to test them, missions three and four are where we can do that deliberately rather than by exclusion here. I agree with that plan and I am not going to manufacture a case against either of them in this discussion. I want to be explicit that I am making no accusation against Arjun, Priya, Theo, or Noah.

Second, the arithmetic, unchanged. Five players, mission two needs three seats. Arjun, Priya, Leo is legal. The cost of rejecting is a new leader, a new proposal, the same absence of information about Theo and Noah, plus one of the four rejections we can afford at most. The cost of approving is at most one of the three failures Evil needs, and we gain a genuine data point on a three-player team.

Third, what I expect the result to tell me, so I am on the record about it now rather than after. If this team succeeds, it says a three-player team including me passed cleanly and it says nothing about the two sitting out. If it fails, it implicates all three of us, and my position will be to examine each of the three honestly, including the two of us who proposed and voted for it, not to assume the proposer and the more vocal advocate are the culprits.

Fourth, on sequencing. I want to note something for later, since it will matter and nobody has raised it yet: with five players, mission three needs only two seats, mission four needs three, mission five needs three. The two-player mission three is the single point where a small, high-signal team can be built, and a failure there carries real weight because a two-person team is more fragile than a three. So I will want that team chosen on the record for what it tests, not for convenience, and I will want to make sure Theo and Noah get a deliberate seat before we reach the three-player missions where excluding them teaches us nothing and costs us information. I am asking for that planning now, not any verdict now.

Priya, your point that mission one produced a clean result but did not verify any individual is correct and I am adopting it as my own standard. The team stands. Approve.

I appreciate Leo's note on sequencing for mission three, and I want to address it now rather than let it drift. Leo is right that mission three in a five-player game is a two-seat team, and that is the highest-leverage moment for the table to test players who have not yet sat on a mission. I want to state my intention clearly: on mission three, I will advocate for a team that gives Theo and Noah a fair opportunity to demonstrate their conduct, because excluding them indefinitely is exactly the kind of pattern that breeds resentment without producing information.

That said, mission two is about building on what mission one showed us. Arjun, Priya, and Leo is a legal three-player team that keeps the tested core together while we gather a second data point on a larger team. Priya's push on my earlier wording was fair and I corrected it. Theo has owned the gap between his public statement and his ballot on mission one, which I find more useful than a clean record would have been. Noah has not spoken on this proposal yet, and I am not reading his silence as suspicion.

I have no accusation against anyone at this table at this point. The public record gives us no evidence to block this lineup, and mission two's result will give us our first look at a three-player team, which is a different and more informative test than mission one's two-person result.

So my position stands: I approve Arjun, Priya, Leo for mission two, and I will look hard at the mission three discussion to make sure the two players who have sat out both missions get their turn on the record.

This is my third and final speaking turn on this proposal, and my position has not moved: I approve Arjun, Priya, Leo for mission two.

First, what is settled. Arjun withdrew "confirmed-good seat" and gave the corrected version — self-knowledge of his own intentions, not public verification. Priya pressed that point and it was answered honestly, which is the standard I applied to myself on mission one. Theo owned the gap between his public statement and his mission one ballot, plainly, without excuses. All three of those are credit on the record, and I am giving it where it is due. I want to be equally explicit about what I am not doing: I am making no accusation against Arjun, Priya, Theo, or Noah. Nobody has produced a piece of evidence against anyone, and I will not manufacture one to look decisive.

Second, the arithmetic, unchanged. Five players, mission two needs three seats. Arjun, Priya, Leo is legal. Rejecting costs a new leader, a new proposal, the same total absence of information about Theo and Noah, plus one of the four rejections we can afford at most. Approving costs at most one of the three failures Evil needs and gives us our first read on a three-player team. Approve is the better trade.

Third, what I expect the result to tell me, stated now rather than after. If this team succeeds, it says a three-player team including me passed cleanly, and it says nothing about the two sitting out. If it fails, it implicates all three of us, and my position will be to examine each of the three honestly, including the two of us who proposed and advocated it, rather than assuming the proposer and the loudest voice are the culprits.

Fourth, the sequencing point I flagged last turn, which I want on the record because it will matter. Mission three in a five-player game needs only two seats. That is the single highest-leverage moment left to test people: a small team where the result is sharp, before the three-player missions where excluding a player teaches us nothing. Arjun has already said he will advocate for Theo and Noah getting a deliberate seat there, and I agree with that. I want that team chosen for what it tests, on the record, not for convenience.

Noah, you are the one player who has not put a position on this proposal in either discussion, and you are also one of the two who will be sitting out a second mission. I am not reading your silence as suspicion — I am reading it as missing information I actually want. Specifically: what is your read on Arjun, Priya, Leo for mission two, and what two-player team do you think should be put up for mission three, and why? If you think this lineup is wrong, say so on the record with a specific reason. I would rather hear a disagreement from you now than guess at it later.

Leo, you asked me directly, so here are my answers on the record.

On Arjun, Priya, Leo for mission two: I approve. The team is legal, it keeps together the three players with the most public reasoning behind them, and nothing in the record justifies blocking it. I want to be precise about what I am basing that on. Mission one returned zero fail cards from Priya and Leo, which is a real result even if it verifies no individual. Arjun withdrew his overstated phrase when Priya pressed it, which is the right way to handle a wording error. And Theo owned the gap between his public statement and his mission one ballot instead of burying it. None of that is proof of anyone's loyalty, but all of it is conduct I can point to, and it is more than I have against any alternative lineup. I have no accusation against anyone at this table, and I am not going to invent one to sound engaged.

On mission three, since you asked for a specific two-player team: I would put up Theo and Priya, or Theo and Leo. My reasoning is the one you and Arjun have already articulated better than I can. Mission three is a two-seat team, which makes it the sharpest test left on the calendar, and Theo is the player with the least tested record and the most explanation owed. Pairing him with someone whose card behavior is on the public record gives the table a clean comparison: if that team fails, the tested partner's record makes the signal much easier to read than a failure among two untested players would. That is also why I would not propose two untested players together on mission three — a fail there would implicate both equally and teach us almost nothing about which one to doubt. I am not married to the exact partner; I am married to the principle that mission three should deliberately test a player who has sat out, paired with a known quantity.

One more thing I want on the record now rather than after the result. If Arjun, Priya, Leo succeeds on mission two, it tells us about the three of them and nothing about me or Theo, and I expect both of us to be on the block for mission three — which I welcome, for the reasons above. If it fails, I will want the table to examine all three seats honestly rather than assume the loudest advocate is the culprit, and I will not rush to judgment on anyone, including the two players I would be sitting out with. I would rather hold everyone, myself included, to the standard Priya set: a result is data, not a verdict.

So: approve on the current proposal, and a deliberate, high-signal team for mission three that finally puts an untested player under the light next to someone we can calibrate against.

Noah, your position on the record is clear and I appreciate the specificity, especially the mission three recommendation. I want to respond to it directly before we close out this discussion.

Your reasoning that mission three's two-seat team is the sharpest test available, and that pairing an untested player with someone whose card behavior we have already seen, is sound. I agree with the principle. Where I would push back gently is on the assumption that the result of mission two tells us nothing about anyone who sat out. That is mostly true, but it does narrow the field: if mission two succeeds, the table has three players with accumulated conduct behind them and two who have produced no mission result at all, and that asymmetry itself is information about where the pressure belongs.

On the current proposal: I approve Arjun, Priya, Leo for mission two. The team is legal, Priya pressed my earlier wording honestly and I corrected it, Theo owned his ballot discrepancy, and now Noah has put a substantive position on the record. The public record supports this lineup and nothing in it justifies a rejection.

I also want to note something the table should hold in mind going into the vote. Theo stated support in discussion on mission one and then voted reject. He has explained it and owned it, which I accept, but the pattern of words not matching ballots is exactly the kind of thing that matters when we start judging mission results. I am not accusing Theo. I am saying the table should watch consistency going forward, from everyone.

My position stands: approve Arjun, Priya, Leo for mission two.

I am still voting approve on Arjun, Priya, Leo for mission two. The team is legal and the public record gives no grounds to block it. Arjun has corrected his wording and Priya has already pressed him on it, so I see no reason to reopen that. Mission one returned zero fail cards, and this lineup keeps the tested players together. I am not accusing anyone. On consistency, I will say my position plainly: I approve this team, and I will judge the mission result when it comes.

I approve Arjun, Priya, Leo for mission two. The proposal is legal, and the public record still gives no evidence that justifies blocking it. Arjun corrected the wording Priya challenged, and the corrected basis — self-knowledge rather than public confirmation — is the honest standard. Leo has reasoned consistently from mission one and has not overstated what the mission result proves. Theo owned the mismatch between his mission-one statement and ballot, and Noah has now put a clear position on the record, including a thoughtful mission-three recommendation. I am not accusing anyone. Mission one's clean result is data, not a verdict on any individual. Mission two gives us the first three-player test, and I will judge the result the same way: if it succeeds, it supports this lineup but does not clear anyone outside it; if it fails, the table should examine all three seats honestly. My vote remains approve on Arjun, Priya, Leo.

I approve Arjun, Priya, and Leo for mission two. The team is legal, Arjun has corrected his wording, and mission one gives no public reason to block this lineup. I have no accusation against anyone. I will judge the result when it comes, and I expect the table to hold every seat to the same standard.

Arjun confirms Arjun, Priya, Leo. The discussion produced no evidence against any member of this lineup. Priya pressed my wording and I corrected it, Theo owned his ballot discrepancy, and Noah put a clear position on the record. Arjun, Priya, Leo remains the legal three-player team built on demonstrated conduct. I am keeping the lineup unchanged.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 2 succeeds (0 fail cards).

Theo proposes Theo, Noah. Mission three is a two-seat team, and Theo and Noah are the two players who have sat out both missions so far, which fits the table's stated plan to give them a deliberate test. Theo is leader and takes the seat himself, so the team stays legal and is easy to defend in discussion.

I am not ready to approve Theo, Noah for mission three. The public record matters here. Missions one and two both succeeded with the Priya-Leo-Arjun core, and the two players now proposed have no mission result at all. That alone is not disqualifying, but the way this team is built cuts against the plan the table discussed: Noah himself said mission three should deliberately test an untested player paired with someone we can calibrate against, and he named Theo with Priya or Theo with Leo. Theo, your proposal pairs the two untested players together, which is the opposite of that principle. If this team fails, it implicates both of you equally and teaches us little about which seat to doubt; if it succeeds, it still tells us nothing about how either of you would perform next to the twice-successful core. I also have to put the ballot record on the table. On mission one and mission two, you stated support in discussion and then voted reject on the final ballot. You owned the first mismatch plainly, which I credited, but the pattern repeated on mission two. That is now a public consistency issue, not a one-off. I am not accusing Noah of anything; my concern is the composition and the leader's explanation. Theo, direct question: given Noah's own mission-three recommendation and your earlier support for a deliberate test, why choose Theo and Noah together, and will you revise to pair one of the untested players with a member of the twice-successful core?

Priya, direct answer. I chose Noah because we are the two players who have sat out both missions so far, and the table agreed that both of us need a deliberate test. If I paired one of us with Priya or Leo, the other would be excluded again, and we would be back to learning nothing about the two players we know least about. Testing us together gives both of us a real result on the same mission. I know Noah suggested pairing an untested player with a core member, and I take that seriously. My answer is that the principle he set out, deliberate testing of someone who has sat out, is exactly what this team does. I have not said I would never revise, but I do not see a reason to change the composition right now. On the ballot question, I already owned my mission one mismatch. I voted reject on mission two because I did not think the lineup had been tested with enough care, and I should have said that in discussion rather than leaving the mismatch for others to find. I am not blaming anyone for raising it. I am asking the table to judge this team on its own composition and on the result. Priya, you have held everyone to the standard that a result is data and not a verdict. I am asking you to apply the same standard here: this team is legal, both members are untested, and mission three will tell us something real about both of us. 2. Roles and private information

Evil players know other Evil players, except Oberon is unknown to the other Evil players and does not know them. The Assassin is an Evil player and makes the final Merlin guess. 3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
